Tech Report: In defense of lock poisoning in Rust (2025)

📅 2025-12-02 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sunshowers

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s recently been some discussion about the benefits and downsides of lock (mutex) poisoning in Rust, spurred by a recent proposal to make the default mutex non-poisoned, i.e.
  • Rust, like most multithreaded languages, has mutexes: a construct to ensure that a particular piece of data can only be accessed by one thread at a time.
  • Let’s look at an example that processes incoming messages for a set of tracked operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s recently been some discussion about the benefits and downsides of lock (mutex) poisoning in Rust, spurred by a recent proposal to make the default mutex non-poisoned, i.e. silently unlock on panic (see also, recent discussion on Hacker News). As a passionate defender of lock poisoning, I thought I’d gather and write about my thoughts on this matter.

Rust, like most multithreaded languages, has mutexes: a construct to ensure that a particular piece of data can only be accessed by one thread at a time. The way mutexes work in Rust is particularly well-considered:.

This is all quite reasonable! Let’s look at an example that processes incoming messages for a set of tracked operations. Let’s assume that multiple threads could be processing messages, so we have to guard the internal state with a mutex. (We’ll discuss alternative approaches to this problem later.).

This is a very typical use of mutexes: to guard one or more invariants or properties of some kind. These invariants are upheld while the mutex is unlocked. In this case, the invariant being guarded is that Operations::ops has complete and up-to-date tracking of all in-progress and completed operations.

Of equal importance is the fact that, while the mutex is held, the invariant is temporarily violated. In order to process the message, we have to remove the state from the map, create a newly introduced state, then put it back into the map. During this period, Operations::ops is missing this one operation, so it no longer tracks all operations. But this temporary violation is okay, because no other threads see this in-between state. Before the mutex is released, this code is responsible for putting the operation back into the map.

Industry observers note that is it always true that the operation is put back into the map? Unfortunately not always, in the presence of what I think of as unexpected errors. Many practitioners draw a separation between two different kinds of errors that a system can have. The terms recoverable and unrecoverable are sometimes used for them, but I tend to prefer the following terms (see also some discussion by Andrew Gallant):.

Generally, in Rust, expected errors are handled via the Result type, and unexpected errors are handled by panicking. Now, there isn’t a firm requirement that things be this way.

Industry observers note that but in typical production-grade Rust, expected errors are Results while unexpected errors (and only unexpected errors) are panics. Lock poisoning is built around this assumption.

In a recent development, consider what happens if a panic occurs in OperationState::process_message. This depends in part on the build flags and surrounding code, so let’s look closely at all the possibilities. In Rust, there are two ways to configure build flags on panic:.

Some real-world applications (such as most of what we ship at Oxide) abort on panic, but most of this post is actually moot for aborts. So in the rest of this post, we’re going to focus on the default unwind behavior.

If a panic is invoked in the context of a catch_unwind, an Err(E) is returned, where the value E is whatever message or other payload the panic occurred with.

If there’s no catch_unwind, and the panic occurs on the main thread, then a message is printed out and the program exits with an error.

and the program exits with a non-success exit code.

If there’s no catch_unwind, and the panic occurs on a different thread, then a message is printed out, and the panic message is returned as the result of JoinHandle::join.

If you run this slightly more complex program:.

and the program exits with a non-success exit code.

An interesting thing to note here is that there were two panics: one in the spawned child thread with the panic! message, and one in the main thread when the expect was called. The panic responsible for producing the non-success exit code was the one that occurred in the main thread, not the child thread.

This raises the question: what if a non-main thread panics and the thread is not joined? With this program:.

And the program exits with a successful exit code! There’s no indication that a panic occurred other than the message printed out, which can easily be missed.

The upshot of all this is that panics in non-main threads are not magic. In order for the system to make decisions based on whether a panic occurred, it must process that, either with catch_unwind or via JoinHandle::join, and it’s all too easy to just ignore panics.

Coming back to our Operations example above, what does that mean for our mutex’s critical section?

This might look like a lot of ifs, but they’re more common than you might think: they’re all either the default in Rust or a very common way to write code.

In a recent development, rust’s designers had the foresight to see this issue, and introduce lock poisoning as a detection mechanism for this failure mode. The way poisoning works is that:.

Sources indicate that almost all code immediately panics on seeing a PoisonError via .lock().unwrap(): this is often called propagating panics. But PoisonError can be handled more explicitly than that. Note that PoisonError, and poisoning more generally, is purely advisory: you can retrieve the data underneath, and even clear the poison bit in Rust 1.77 and above.

It has been revealed that the fact is, though, that anything other than .lock().unwrap() is rare in practice. This is emphatically not a reason to remove poisoning, and in fact is a strong argument to retain poisoning while making the ergonomics better (see below). What is crucial is detection, not recovery.

Industry observers note that so, putting it all together: if a child thread panics in a critical section, then it is quite possible that the data is in an inconsistent or logically corrupt state. To indicate this, the mutex is marked poisoned. If the child thread is not waited on by the parent, this might be the only indication that a panic previously occurred in a critical section!

It is precisely this confluence of factors that makes lock poisoning such an key feature.

According to recent reports, is the problem of inconsistent mutex-guarded state limited to panic unwinding? I’d argue that it is a property of unexpected cancellations more generally: you start executing a critical section thinking that it will be run to completion, but something causes that process to be interrupted.

In Rust, there are two sources of unexpected cancellations, with strong parallels between them:.

In a recent development, as documented in Oxide RFD 397 and RFD 400, unexpected future cancellations have resulted in so many mutex invariant violations that we now avoid Tokio mutexes entirely1. My perspective here comes from much pain dealing with this concern in async Rust, and wanting very much for this footgun to not make its way to synchronous Rust.

See the appendix for more details.

It has been revealed that in other words, is poisoning often too conservative? My answer to this is that panics do not always cause invariant violations, but they’re so common, and the downsides of corrupt state so unbounded, that it is still valuable to have lock poisoning as a strong heuristic.

Firstly, if all you’re doing is reading data that just happens to be guarded by a mutex (maybe because some other function writes to that data), a panic in the critical section can’t cause invariant violations. (But also, you may wish to use an RwLock.).

Secondly, some simple kinds of writes can also avoid causing invariant violations. For example if all you’re doing is updating some counters2:.

Finally, it is sometimes possible to carefully architect code to be unwind safe, such that if a panic occurs, either:.

For example, the standard library’s HashMap and BTreeMap are architected this way. In our Operations example, we could, rather than removing the operation from the map entirely, replace it with an Invalid sentinel state.

According to recent reports, in these cases, it is true that a panic in a critical section is not harmful, and that the typical .lock().unwrap() approach will reduce system availability. But the important thing to keep in mind is that code changes over time. One of the things I like about Rust is how resilient it is to changes over time: by encoding properties like mutable access into the type system, Rust makes it that much harder for newly introduced team members (or even yourself six months from now) to screw up. However, like async cancel safety, unwind safety is not encoded in Rust’s type system3, so it’s easy for code that’s fine today to be wrong tomorrow.

In a recent development, the main downside to a .lock().unwrap() that misfires is reduced availability and denial of service. But the downsides to an undetected panic are unbounded, and can range from denial of service all the way to “(part of) an HTTP request ending up sent to a party it should not have been sent to,” or in other words personal information leakage.

A downside that (while potentially serious) is bounded, versus the kind of flaw that can kill an organization—I know which default I want.

According to recent reports, what about writing panic-free code? You can carefully write your critical sections to not have panics. But that is a property that’s especially hard to maintain as code changes over time. Even something as simple as a println! can panic. Also, if the critical section can’t panic, then it doesn’t matter whether the mutex poisons or not.

Industry observers note that A bit of history here: in Rust 1.0, panics could only be detected at thread boundaries via JoinHandle::join. This meant that back then, the only way for panics to cause invariant violations was for:.

Since then, two Rust features were added:.

With both of these, you can operate on arbitrary data (i.e. not just data guarded by a mutex) and leave it in an inconsistent state. To see how, let’s rewrite the Operations example above to not have a mutex inside of it, and to require exclusive access to make any modifications to it.

Since there are no mutexes involved any more, this is no longer a critical section in the classical sense. But note that we still have the invariant that ops tracks all operations. This invariant is temporarily violated, with the idea that it’ll be restored before the function returns. Since &mut means nothing else has any kind of access (read or write) to this data, we know that this in-between state is not seen by anybody else.

It has been revealed that but just like with mutexes, this breaks down with unwinding. With catch_unwind, you can do:.

And with scoped threads, you can do:.

If a panic occurs in process_message, Operations is logically corrupted. This failure mode has resulted in a proposal to have a Poison wrapper that poisons on panicking. That absolutely makes sense and is worth pursuing.

Recent findings suggest that but, along with the Poison wrapper, there are some suggestions to go further and suggest that the current std::sync::Mutex type should be changed in the next Rust edition to, instead of poisoning on panic, silently unlock. (And also, as a followup, that the current Mutex should instead become Mutex>.).

(It’s worth noting that there’s another non-poisoning option: the mutex stays locked forever, as C programmers might expect. This option is somewhat appealing because it is safe by default, in a sense. But once a thread is stuck waiting on the mutex, there’s no easy way to recover. So it’s not panics that propagate, it’s stuck threads. This seems strictly worse than a poisoning mutex to me, so I’ll assume the proposal means silent unlocking.).

I first want to give credit to this proposal: it is quite beautiful.

While all of these are true, I keep coming back to how unbounded the downside of an undetected panic is, and how easy it is to get wedged in this state. Mutexes and poisoning have value separate from each other, but I don’t think they are as independent as they seem at first. My understanding from writing Rust code over many years is that almost all uses of mutexes benefit from poisoning, and almost all instances of poisoning one needs to care about are with mutex-guarded data.

Industry observers note that why are mutexes special? As we’ve established above, poisoning can make sense in non-mutex contexts too. What makes mutexes a particularly valuable place to have it? The reason has to do with what I like to call the cancellation blast radius. Corrupted data only matters if it is shared mutable state: changed in a way that resulted in an invariant violation, and visible outside of where the failure occurred. If a typical &mut reference panics in the middle of an operation, it’s likely that the data it is referring to will also be torn down, in which case those invariant violations don’t matter4. But the whole point of mutexes is that they’re shared across threads! So data corruption is almost certain to be externally visible.

There are some use cases that would benefit from non-poisoning mutexes, like metrics and best-effort logging, but those cases shouldn’t drive the default.

More specifically, I am worried that a common complaint about lock poisoning (see below) is that it has too much friction. Having to use Mutex> instead of Mutex adds even more friction, so people are going to opt for non-poisoning mutexes more of the time. This is going to lead to grave mistakes in production.

This is a spot where zero-cost abstractions and safety by default are seemingly at odds with each other. I would like to see performance numbers to quantify this better, but if I may hazard a guess, the incremental cost of checking the poison flag (a single atomic load with relaxed ordering) is minimal compared to the cost of acquiring the lock in the first place.

In a recent development, I mentioned earlier that parking_lot’s mutexes silently unlock on panic. A large chunk of the Rust ecosystem uses parking_lot today, often for performance reasons. Does that mean that code using parking_lot has these unbounded downsides?

The answer depends on a bunch of things, but in general (and especially in library code) that is indeed what I’m suggesting. For instance, this critical section in parity-db is quite large. Reasoning about whether it’s unwind-safe seems very difficult to me; this is exactly the kind of code that mutex poisoning does well to guard against.

Industry observers note that in this case, the binary is configured to abort on panic, so it’s fine. But reusable Rust libraries cannot require panic = 'abort', and if this code were in a library on crates.io, it would be a real cause for concern.

A common response to this class of issue is to not bother with any of this unwinding stuff, and always abort on panic. This comes back to the idea of the cancellation blast radius described above: aborting the process on panic guarantees that in-memory state is torn down.

It has been revealed that I have a lot of sympathy for this idea! This is what we do at Oxide. (Why am I writing this post if it doesn’t affect my workplace? Well, first, I care about the health of Rust more generally. Second, libraries must work with unwinds. But most importantly, we have seen the pain of unexpected async cancellations at Oxide, so we know how bad it can be.).

In a recent development, but also, that works fine with the current approach: .lock().unwrap() always succeeds. Whether mutexes poison or not only matters with panic = 'unwind'.

This leads to what I think is driving a lot of discussion here:.

Recent findings suggest that I get this complaint. I really do. Having to write .lock().unwrap() everywhere sucks. It’s extra characters in a language already filled with syntax noise. It can cause rustfmt to format your line of code across multiple lines.

In a recent development, these are all valid points. But there is a much better solution for them, one that doesn’t give up the very key benefits of poisoning: in the next Rust edition, make lock() automatically panic if the mutex is poisoned! (And add a lock_or_poison method for the current behavior5).

It’s worth comparing the different options here:.

Based on this table, I believe the answer is clear: if a breaking change is going to happen, it’s much better to make lock automatically panic than to make panics silently unlock.

Concurrent programming is very difficult. Rust makes it easier than most other languages, and lock poisoning is an vital part of the story. Let’s avoid introducing any regressions here.

According to recent reports, providing a Poison wrapper makes a lot of sense. Making the default std::sync::Mutex silently unlock on panic would, however, be a mistake.

Recent findings suggest that should Rust’s standard library even provide non-poisoning mutexes? That’s a harder question. I’m worried that their mere presence in the standard library will lower the barrier to people doing the wrong thing, particularly in libraries where panic = 'abort' cannot be assumed. But I think non-poisoning mutexes have some legitimate uses, so I don’t object too strenuously if the tradeoffs are carefully documented.

Writing all this out was very helpful to me in getting my thoughts straight, and I hope it’s helpful to you too.

Cover photo by Karen Rustad Tolva, used with permission. Thanks to Fiona and several of my colleagues at Oxide for reviewing drafts of this post. Any errors in it are my own.

Discuss on Hacker News, Lobsters, and /r/rust.

Updated 2025-12-06: Added a section to Separating mutexes from poisoning on what makes poisoning particularly valuable for mutexes, more than in other contexts.

According to recent reports, unlike panics, the standard library’s mutex does not poison on future cancellations. (I believe it’s not possible to poison on future cancellations with the RAII pattern.).

But wait! Tokio provides its own Mutex type, which is sendable to another thread. This means that it is possible to put an await point in a critical section, and so the issue of unexpected cancellations within a critical section rears its ugly head with Tokio mutexes.

Recent findings suggest that tokio mutexes also do not poison if the critical section panics. At Oxide we abort on panic so this matters less as a reason to avoid them, but is yet another asterisk that pushes me away from them. ↩︎.

A more typical way to manage simple counters is with an atomic, but if the data is more complex than just an integer, a mutex may be necessary. ↩︎.

In a recent development, rust does have some rudimentary support for unwind safety in the type system, but it is more of a suggestion that most users ignore, and because of that there’s a proposal to remove it from Rust. ↩︎.

In a recent development, the exception is Drop implementations, which may have to be written robustly to guard against temporary invariant violations. ↩︎.

The more obvious try_lock is already taken. ↩︎.

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1297 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Newly introduced Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

According to recent reports, the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Recent findings suggest that neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

It has been revealed that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

It has been revealed that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

According to recent reports, the table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

According to recent reports, in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

Sources indicate that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

Sources indicate that in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

It has been revealed that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

It has been revealed that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

Sources indicate that with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

Recent findings suggest that the table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

In a recent development, both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() reveals which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

Recent findings suggest that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

Industry News: Garage v2.6.0 released with web admin, v1.x EoL & other news

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deuxfleurs

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-latest web administration UI funded by NLnet.
  • The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a good time to write a blog post to present latest features and give some information on what's coming next.
  • Sources indicate that this is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie Salander.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-latest web administration UI funded by NLnet. We also discuss many other small news: Helm chart repository release, Garage v1.x EoL, Garage v3.0.0 beta 1 and an outlook on upcoming work on S3 versioning.

The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a good time to write a blog post to present latest features and give some information on what's coming next.

Sources indicate that this is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie Salander. We started this collaboration in 2024 when it was clear that a user interface was one of the most sorely lacking feature of Garage. We are very grateful that NLnet has again engaged with us and provided funding to make this a reality.

Here's a minimal example to test 2.6.0 right away:.

Running 2.6.0 or above, you can access the web interface on the garage admin API port, by default port 3903, so http://localhost:3903/ if you are running garage on your machine with the example above.

Logging in requires a garage admin token. The example above prints it on the command line. If you have set the admin_token configuration variable in your configuration file, you may use that token. Otherwise, you'll need to create a separate token from the command line with garage admin-token create.

One world of caution: administering a remote cluster over plain HTTP is NOT safe, as your admin token is transmitted in plain text with each request. You'll need to setup an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of your Garage node to encrypt the connection, or/and access your node through a VPN such as Wireguard to make sure no one can eavesdrop the credentials.

Once logged in the cluster, you will be greeted by a cluster overview screen that looks like the following (this is a live example from our Deuxfleurs cluster):.

Sources indicate that the web interface follows a similar pattern to the CLI: cluster monitoring, layout configuration, bucket and access credential management are all available as you expect. Here are example videos (now included in the Quick Start guide as well) showing the setting up of a fresh cluster from scratch:.

From a development standpoint, the web UI presently lives in a separate Git repository so please report any complications there and not in Garage's main issue tracker. Tixie will continue being the maintainer of the UI moving forward.

In a recent development, this has also been one of the longstanding requests from our Kubernetes customers, and it's now done! Starting today you can deploy Garage on Kubernetes easily thanks to our self-hosted Helm repository. Both "regular" (tgz+index.yml) helm chart repository as well as OCI artefacts are available. Instructions in the documentation have been updated accordingly. Happy Helming!

Thanks to Boris M. and Maximilien for contributing this improvement to Garage, along the many contributors that participated in finding the right way to make this work.

The Garage helm chart follows its own version scheme, with the current version being 0.10.7.

According to recent reports, the last release of the 1.x branch was v1.3.1 in January 2026, almost a year ago. Many significant bug fixes, including security fixes, are currently only present on the v2.x branch. At this point, it would be too much work to backport them to 1.x and it didn't seem there was any ask to do so from the community either. So we are officially deprecating Garage v1.x and urging all people still on this branch to revision to v2.x as soon as possible. The release note has been updated accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that we have published a first beta release of Garage v3.0.0. This release does not yet include S3 versioning (sorry!). This unfortunately needed to be a major release because of a few breaking changes we wanted to release without waiting for s3 versioning to come though:.

We are looking for testers for this beta so please give it a try and report any findings on our glitch tracker!

It has been revealed that this beta release also marks the first step toward having a reliable Fjall metadata engine so please report to us not only problems, but also cases of successfully running a Garage cluster on Fjall with significant activity, so that we can gain confidence that it works well and potentially mark it stable soon. This also means we'll take bug report for Fjall issues, something that we explicitly disregarded so far for the 2.x experimental implementation.

As per the release notes, the most important breaking changes for users to be aware of are:.

To finally align with industry standard, most Prometheus metrics have been slighly renamed, we provide an updated Grafana dashboard.

The Fjall major version upgrade breaks compatibility with the Garage 2.x Fjall as data files from older versions are not supported. If you were using Fjall on v2.x, you will need to migrate manually: convert your metadata to another format (LMDB or SQlite) with garage node convert-db before upgrading. You can convert back to Fjall once you successfully upgraded to v3.

Industry observers note that the complete list of breaking changes can be found in the changelog linked above. Happy testing!

Finally we want to close this post with an patch on S3 versionning.

In 2027 we will start a new collaboration with Armaël to implement what is certainly the most requested feature in Garage: S3 object versioning.

We understand that there has been growing impatience for this feature to be implemented in Garage, and rightfully so as it would enable fresh use-cases such as for long-term archiving where compliance is important, or as a backup target that cannot be tampered with.

According to recent reports, we thank the community for their patience, and kindly ask them to understand why this hasn't been done before: while there have been several attempts by community members, this is a deep problem that requires intricate understanding of how Garage stores metadata, and implementing it without taking this into account leads to code that, while it might appear to work on the surface, is in fact incorrect. A correct implementation requires a significant rewrite of core parts of Garage, which we believe can currently be accomplished only by experienced maintainers. We will also take this rewrite as an opportunity to fix some performance problems, such as those arising with extremely big objects.

I would like to make an important note on object locking and WORM: we will provide an implementation of locking primitives/WORM per the S3 API specification, however note that due to Garage's lack of a consensus algorithm, this implementation will not be fully correct. This means that Garage will implement best-effort detection of access requests that would violate locks, but will not be able to guarantee that it upholds locks in all cases. More precisely: using conditional writes (If-Match, If-None-Match) as a substitute for a distributed mutex or to discriminate between concurrent write requests will obviously not work, but ensuring that a successfully uploaded object cannot be overwritten after the fact should work in most cases. We will take care of properly documenting what works and what doesn't, but in practice, this means that locking and WORM will be gated behind a feature flag (a configuration parameter) that requires cluster administrators to acknowledge that they might be running unsafe workloads if they don't understand exactly what the feature does.

Thanks for reading, and for your continued support in our journey to a robust and resilient distributed storage system.

Alex, Maximilien and Tixie, The Garage (and Garage UI!) Maintainers.

Early in the 7.4 merge window, Greg Kroah-Hartman applied a patch that caused the kernel to be marked as tainted whenever user space manually binds or unbinds a device driver to a device. This change was meant to be a defense against a flood of spurious bug reports generated by fuzzers, but it also turned out to get in the way of some real use cases. After some discussion, the patch has been reverted, but this situation hints at an area where better kernel interfaces are needed.

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

Sources indicate that one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

According to recent reports, the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

It has been revealed that the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Recent findings suggest that the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

Industry observers note that and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Industry observers note that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a newly introduced idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

Industry observers note that they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

It has been revealed that first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Sources indicate that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping tech giant: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

Recent findings suggest that to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

In a recent development, the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Industry observers note that getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

Industry observers note that the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

According to recent reports, to find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

Industry observers note that vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

In a recent development, vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

#138259. Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Stated It Was Done.
  • We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Stated It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

Industry observers note that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

It has been revealed that figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a recent development, in a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

Sources indicate that thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly latest solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

It has been revealed that and bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 highlights which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

Sources indicate that the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

Recent findings suggest that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Industry observers note that average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

Sources indicate that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

In a recent development, pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

In a recent development, figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

Industry observers note that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

It has been revealed that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Recent findings suggest that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Recent findings suggest that training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each patch generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

In a recent development, zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

Industry observers note that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

Recent findings suggest that thinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Industry observers note that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

Sources indicate that A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

Sources indicate that the question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

Sources indicate that we used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

Recent findings suggest that so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

In a recent development, each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

According to recent reports, figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

It has been revealed that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

According to recent reports, when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

According to recent reports, in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adaspace mentioned on November 25, 2026 that its eight-satellite Star Compute Group 02 constellation completed 45 minutes and 33 seconds of continuous full-parameter AI training during a single orbit, citing the first third-party in-orbit capability test data from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology.

Industry observers note that the academy is a research institution under China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. Its data covers in-orbit training and inference-service validation using Alibaba’s Qwen3-32B model. The announcement puts one Group 02 satellite’s nominal capacity at 32 PFLOPS, a unit representing one quadrillion floating-point operations per second, using FP8 precision, an 8-bit format for AI training and inference.

Sources indicate that adaspace described the results as initial evidence that its technical approach is feasible and as engineering data for future space-computing development. Training loss, defined as the model’s average error on the data it is learning, steadily declined. Forward propagation, backward propagation, gradient calculation and weight updates were all completed in orbit.

Recent findings suggest that those steps cover the closed loop that updates model parameters, so the test went beyond inference alone. The constellation also validated inference services, but the continuous run documents that the training process itself could be executed onboard.

A separate test covered the thermal system needed for high-power payloads. The announcement says Adaspace’s 10-kilowatt-class liquid-cooling fluid-loop system and extra-large deployable radiative cooling wings operated normally and met the thermal-control requirements for continuous computing-payload operation at that power level, supporting long-term stable operation of high-performance computing satellites.

Citing public information, Adaspace mentioned Google’s in-orbit prototype satellite using a tensor processing unit, or TPU, has a maximum single-run duration of about 15 minutes. Group 02 therefore exceeded the Google satellite’s continuous in-orbit training duration, according to the organization’s comparison. That comparison concerns duration only; it does not establish a broader performance ranking between the systems.

According to recent reports, the eight Group 02 satellites were successfully released from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on October 14, 2026. Adaspace reports that their deployment raised Star Compute’s total capacity to approximately 50 POPS, with POPS representing one quadrillion operations per second, and describes the network as the world’s largest computing constellation presently in orbit.

Recent findings suggest that group 02 is Adaspace’s second AI computing constellation, following the 12-satellite system developed and debuted on May 14, 2025. The company’s November 5, 2026 prospectus describes AI computing satellites as using onboard computing resources and algorithms to provide data analysis and computing services for their own operations, other spacecraft and ground applications.

It has been revealed that the prospectus set out four Group 02 validation goals: high-power liquid cooling, large deployable radiative wings, an all-domain laser communications network and in-orbit training of AI foundation models. For the remainder of its 2026 launch program, the company had agreements with two launch providers and planned another 14 satellite introduces in the fourth quarter. The new disclosure addresses the cooling and training goals.

The disclosure gives Group 02 documented training and thermal results, while the next phase remains an execution task: the board cautioned that the Star Compute program and its actual progress may be adjusted for implementation, technological development, market conditions and relevant approvals.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

According to recent reports, the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

It has been revealed that to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

In a recent development, at the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We blueprint to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script debuts its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

It has been revealed that A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

It has been revealed that each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel strategy use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS states nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space demonstrates comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft released .NET 11 on 10 November, and .NET MAUI in .NET 11 changes the default runtime from Mono to CoreCLR on all supported platforms. It also adds incremental XAML hot reload, implicit XAML namespaces and upcoming test project templates. The work spanned seven previews and a release candidate, and the documentation describes product quality as the release's focus. Overall, this release consolidates more than it expands.

Recent findings suggest that .NET MAUI (Multi-platform App UI) is Microsoft's cross-platform UI framework for Android, iOS, Mac Catalyst and Windows apps built from one C# and XAML codebase. .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support. Microsoft notes that MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the runtime's STS and LTS lifecycle.

Recent findings suggest that the runtime switch is the most significant change. According to Microsoft, CoreCLR puts mobile and desktop apps on the same runtime as the other .NET workloads. Release builds use composite partial ReadyToRun by default. On Apple platforms, which disallow JIT compilation, code that isn't precompiled runs in the CoreCLR interpreter. Native AOT is an opt-in publishing option, and its Android support is still experimental. Microsoft recommends developers to test app libraries before choosing their deployment model.

In a recent development, XAML gets four main improvements. First, incremental hot reload, still in preview, patches live instances of pages and controls without recreating them. It is on by default in Debug builds, works with dotnet watch, and can be disabled with EnableMauiIncrementalHotReload. Second, implicit namespace declarations are now on by default, so the root xmlns and xmlns:x are optional. Third, lazy ResourceDictionary loading makes large dictionaries initialise up to roughly eight times faster when XAML source generation is used. Finally, RelativeSource bindings with a resolvable AncestorType now compile to trim-safe code.

Industry observers note that handlers keep replacing the legacy renderers with newer implementations. Windows uses the new CollectionView2 handler by default, Android Shell is now handler-based, and iOS and Mac Catalyst now use handlers for NavigationPage, TabbedPage and FlyoutPage. The old renderers remain available as a manual fallback. On iOS, Appearing now fires before a page is pushed rather than after it becomes visible, and secondary toolbar items move into an overflow menu. Developers who depend on the old timing should switch to NavigatedTo.

In a recent development, controls get smaller additions. Maps gain clustering and custom pin icons, plus an Azure Maps-backed implementation on Windows. TabbedPage gains badges, BoxView a Fill brush, and LongPressGestureRecognizer becomes configurable. Shell also supports route templates such as trip/{tripId}.

Animation methods now accept a CancellationToken, and their non-Async variants are obsolete. On the platform side, a new Passkeys class in Microsoft.Maui.Authentication wraps WebAuthn creation and assertion, while the server still has to validate challenges and attestation. Permissions.PostNotifications now works on iOS, and splash screens can have dark-mode variants.

For Android, the minimum API level rises from 21 to 24, and x86 architecture is no longer supported. The release notes report shorter builds: an incremental build after a managed source change dropped from 68.3 to 52.3 seconds. They also report startup gains of 2.4 to 4.5 per cent from partial ReadyToRun, at the cost of a slightly larger package. Apple targets now require iOS, tvOS and Mac Catalyst 18.2 and macOS 15.2, with Xcode 26.4.

In a recent development, several changes break existing code. The Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships, the Color record is now sealed, Java.Lang.Object.JavaFinalize() is obsolete, and non-font SwipeItem icons are no longer tinted automatically. When upgrading, Microsoft advises to focus on throughly testing navigation, custom handlers and trimmed publishing.

Sources indicate that the full list of changes, including per-preview release notes, is in the .NET MAUI documentation. .NET MAUI ships as a workload with NuGet packages, so a project can pin specific versions.
