📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.
  • Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally crucial legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.
  • Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally crucial legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.

Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.

That's the assessment of researchers at Bay Area Labs, who this week flagged five particularly popular digital extensions that allow Brazilian citizens and institutions to not only sign official documents, but sign them with the greatest possible degree of trust issued by their government. All five of them possessed vulnerabilities which could've allowed attacker-controlled websites to run arbitrary code on users' machines.

Recent findings suggest that one can only hope that the researchers, who disclosed the vulnerabilities this week, were the first to discover them. Remote code execution (RCE) in this context could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names, and hackers to breach major government organizations (as well as professionals who manage large amounts of personal, financial, tax, and health information on behalf of their clients).

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc.

In a recent development, on Sept. 23, 2020, Brazil's National Congress enacted Federal Law No. 14,063. 14,063 laid the ground rules on how individuals and organizations could digitally sign documents when dealing with public institutions. Among other things, it delineated three tiers of trust that an electronic signature could carry: "simple," "advanced," and "qualified." "Qualified" meant that a digital signature would be equivalent to a notarized, handwritten one. It would be sufficient for high-stakes legal proceedings, like real estate transfers and electronic tax processes. And any digital signature backed with an ICP-Brasil certificate — ICP-Brasil is the country's official national public key infrastructure (PKI) framework — would be considered "qualified.".

Brazilian government institutions, tax professionals, and anyone in-between who wants to provide a qualified digital signature for a sensitive legal document online can use browser extensions like Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital. Each of these tools lets official government and vendor portals read ICP-Brasil certificates, to confirm that signers are who they say they are, and put pen to Web page.

These tools will also engage with non-official websites. So if an attacker can lure a victim to their own site — or, in some cases, plant a malicious ad or iframe on a legitimate site — they can engage that victim's authentication middleware. Only one of the five extensions, CertiPlugin, had any kind of allowlist, yet it included any domain ending in ".one," meaning that an attacker would simply need to purchase a domain with that common and freely available suffix in order to perform an attack.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era.

According to recent reports, the core issue endemic to each of these five extensions, and others used by other national governments, is that they allow websites to dictate the dynamic link libraries (DLLs) they load. Loading cryptographic libraries is a normal part of the way these apps work. But if they don't properly check that a loaded file is trusted? In that case, an attacker that lures a victim to their site can trigger a malware download and then instruct the victim's signing software to load that malware as if it were a legitimate library.

All five extensions' RCE vulnerabilities earned "critical" 9.6 scores in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Each of them was patched as of mid-September, but lessons remain.

Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have more than 10 million installs between them.

Industry observers note that among that user base are some of the most significant, high-value organizations and professionals in the country. On its website, Lacuna alone counts Brazil's Federal Senate, its National Council of Justice, its navy, and its stock exchange among its clients "who trust our work." These extensions are far from limited to major government agencies, of course. BRy advertises its work with the University of São Paulo, the São Paulo metro, and one of the country's few biggest banks, Caixa Econômica Federal.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem.

Attackers could have used the vulnerable authentication middleware to infect employees at major state institutions and, in Arnott's words, "cause mayhem." As an easier alternative, they could target middle class professionals: lawyers, doctors, accountants and so on. An accountant might manage digital signing credentials for hundreds of different individuals and businesses on their single computer. An attacker with that accountant's access could then impersonate those people and companies in legally significant transactions — forging agreements, submitting false tax filings ... the sky's the limit.

Recent findings suggest that "It's really interesting how these signing tools always consistently have the same critical vulnerabilities," Arnott marvels, after having found characteristically similar vulnerabilities in extensions used by Belgium, Sweden, and Qatar's governments in recent months. "Since they are security tools, you'd expect them to be properly built. But they're so often making the same mistake, by allowing any site to pick which DLLs to load. I imagine it's to reduce friction so organizations can more easily load in the drivers for hardware security tokens and readers, because the driver DLLs aren't always known to the signing tool vendor or signed properly with Authenticode. It is insane to me how many independent vendors make this same mistake though.".

A product team can ship the same model to two customers and inherit two different compliance problems. One customer uses it to draft internal notes; another uses it in a consequential decision. The technology may look similar while the legal role, evidence requirements and affected people change.

That is what makes AI regulation an operating challenge in 2027. Businesses will need a usable account of where the product may go, what it may do there and which obligations travel with the use case.

Recent findings suggest that the timetable itself requires care. The European Commission notes the AI Omnibus entered into force in July 2026. Its current AI Act FAQ distinguishes high-risk application dates, including December 2, 2027 for Annex III systems and August 2, 2028 for certain product-related systems. Older summaries can therefore mislead planning. These forecasts use the position available on November 3, 2026; subsequent legal changes could alter the calendar.

The promise of one global product will increasingly require a more detailed release package. In 2027, suppliers will publish market-specific configurations or documents that distinguish the customer's role and intended use. The underlying model can remain shared. What changes is the precision with which the company explains the conditions under which the finished service can be offered.

One underlying model can support many products, and one product can create different obligations depending on its purpose, users and deployment location. A general writing assistant and an employment-screening system do not become equivalent simply because they share model infrastructure.

It has been revealed that the Commission's explanation of AI Act scope distinguishes providers, deployers and general-purpose model suppliers, including some actors outside the EU whose products enter its market. That role-based structure makes a single undifferentiated global compliance statement increasingly difficult to use.

My expectation is practical differentiation: market-specific documentation, transparency settings, intended-use boundaries and enterprise support. This need not require separate models for every country. Over-separating the technical stack can itself create maintenance and testing problems. The more likely architecture is a shared product with explicit regional conditions and a controlled process for deciding which configurations may be sold where.

Look for documentation that identifies the jurisdiction, product role and applicable use case. Regional server hosting by itself would not establish this forecast. A meaningful compliance package should explain which obligations it supports and what the customer still needs to do.

In a recent development, map market access requirements onto the release process before promising worldwide availability. In 2027, buyers of EU high-risk applications will ask earlier for operational evidence. That will move compliance discussion into demonstrations, acceptance criteria and contracts, where the customer can still influence what is delivered.

The Commission's enforcement overview distinguishes the responsibilities of authorities and the timing of obligations. The Council's AI Act timeline also records the evolving implementation sequence. These official materials describe the legal framework; they do not prove that every supplier is ready.

The Council's implementation timeline identifies the revised timetable for national sandboxes. The Commission FAQ explains their role in supporting innovation. Sources indicate that the difference between the 2026 Omnibus change and earlier implementation summaries illustrates the operational problem. 📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
  • We've been very happy with the reception so far.
  • Sources indicate that most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Sources indicate that most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of customers, not how much speech you generate.

It has been revealed that getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

Sources indicate that we announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early customers. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Sources indicate that phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created newly introduced challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Industry observers note that phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the notable things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

In a recent development, it runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a newly introduced inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

According to recent reports, it belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

According to recent reports, phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

In a recent development, we also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

It has been revealed that phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Recent findings suggest that congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review.

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read.

Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track at QCon San Francisco 2026, Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, argued that line-by-line code review is already quietly dead on most teams, and that the sharper question is "how long until we stop reading the code?" He also flagged his conflict of interest up front, noting that he runs a tech giant that sells a solution and asking the audience to "be suspicious of me.".

The talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space in March 2026 proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews. Eight months on, Jain stated the mechanics held up but the essay missed human judgment entirely. He began with the data that unseated his original framing. A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation, yet only 14% of their comments were actually about defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews reached almost the same split. Code review was never really about bugs, he argued, it was about knowledge sharing, echoing Addy Osmani: "We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been.".

A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found that over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year. Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines, yet the median PR today is 640 lines. "We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it," Jain remarked, pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated PRs that collected over 1,900 upvotes. The result is "review theater," where agents write, another AI reviews, agents revise, and humans skim and merge.

Recent findings suggest that to replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers: Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own. Agents should argue about a change locally before the PR exists, surfacing only what they disagreed about. Intent and acceptance criteria, familiar from behaviour-driven development, should be captured during the coding session and attached to the PR rather than discarded. Repeated review comments become invariants, standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method, and a team owner. Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants. Evidence should replace green checks: screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies, and database logs, because the same agent that wrote the code likely wrote its unit tests. Humans then debate decisions rather than diffs, and ownership shifts from author and reviewer to the teams that own the rules.

In a recent development, jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs it did a year ago and still approves every one, while reverts have dropped around 40%. He also shared a failure: a change passed every filter and caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, after which the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it. Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still get line-by-line review.

Sources indicate that he closed with a line: You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

  • Threat reporting on Iran typically covers one campaign at a time, and vendors track the same groups under different names.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Analysis of 20 Iranian state-sponsored threat groups details how espionage, ransomware, and hacktivism intersect in state-backed cyber campaigns.

ANTA CLARA, Calif. — (BUSINESS WIRE) — AttackIQ, the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), today released upcoming research that connects previously fragmented reporting on individual Iranian cyber campaigns to map the relationships among state-sponsored operators and the institutions supporting them. The findings show Iranian espionage groups turn compromised networks into launchpads for other operators, transforming intelligence-gathering operations into destructive attacks.

Threat reporting on Iran typically covers one campaign at a time, and vendors track the same groups under different names. Helix Kitten alone appears under eight other names, including OilRig, APT34 and Scarred Manticore. AttackIQ’s Adversary Research Team consolidated that reporting into Weighing Cyber Power: Evaluating the Strategic and Operational Significance of Iran’s State-Sponsored Cyber Capability, a single map of 20 Iranian adversaries, the government institutions they are linked to and the contractors that supply their personnel, tooling and infrastructure.

Related:Attackers Target .NET Developers With Poisoned Job Assessments.

“The value of threat research is measured by the decisions it informs,” mentioned Paul Reid, VP of Adversary Research at AttackIQ. “Understanding which Iranian groups work together, and how confident we can be in each relationship, gives defenders a clear starting point for emulation and a realistic picture of what could follow an initial compromise. It turns a single detection into a forecast of what comes next.”.

The report traces how a single intrusion can pass between groups. In one documented case, Helix Kitten (Scarred Manticore), conducted prolonged intelligence collection inside a network before handing off the network access to Banished Kitten (Void Manticore), which pursued destructive objectives. In a second case, Static Kitten (Mango Sandstorm) established access and passed it to Storm-1084, a destructive operator. In a separate campaign against the Albanian government, four separately tracked groups contributed to the same operation, which spanned reconnaissance, initial access, data theft and the deployment of destructive tooling.

Recent findings suggest that when the damage arrives, it is frequently disguised. The research also found Iranian groups staging destructive attacks as ransomware or hacktivism, obscuring the intent behind the attacks. Pioneer Kitten provided criminal ransomware affiliates with access to compromised networks.

The organizations hit first may be a route to other targets. Several groups can gain access to more heavily defended organizations, including in the defense industrial base, through their subsidiaries, contractors, and suppliers.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge.

It has been revealed that the analysis classifies 20 Iranian adversaries into three weight classes based on their organizational significance, operational relevance, and demonstrated capabilities. The classifications underscore that even smaller, specialized groups can play critical roles in larger cyber campaigns.

Heavyweight: Established groups with sustained espionage operations, internally developed tooling and a central role in Iran’s cyber strategy.

Lightweight: Groups with more focused missions, including specialized espionage, access facilitation and destructive operations.

Featherweight: Groups with narrower or less consistently documented activity, some relying on support from more established adversaries.

“Iran isn’t as technically sophisticated as China, Russia or North Korea, but what it lacks in sophistication it makes up for in cadence,” mentioned Francis Guibernau, Senior Adversary Research Engineer at AttackIQ. “They target anything and everything, on every operating system and in industrial environments. That volume, combined with how freely these groups share access, is what makes the ecosystem dangerous.”.

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline.

In a recent development, the research draws on more than 200 references and consolidates more than 2,600 procedures, 1,300 file indicators, and 2,300 network indicators. The analysis was also validated against threat intelligence and real-world activity observed by several Fortune 150 companies actively targeted by Iranian threat actors. The research team also received input from National Computer Incident Response Teams (CIRTs) and members of the intelligence community.

To help organizations put the research into practice, AttackIQ will be releasing adversary emulations based on the documented tactics, techniques, and procedures of Iranian threat actors over the coming weeks. These emulations will enable security teams to safely test their defenses against relevant adversary behaviors, identify gaps in detection and prevention, and prioritize improvements based on real-world threat intelligence.

For a closer look at the findings with AttackIQ’s adversary research team, join the December 10 webinar, Breaking Down Iran’s Most Dangerous Cyber Tactics.

AttackIQ is the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), helping organizations continuously validate defenses, break attack paths, and reduce threat debt through evidence-based security operations.

Through AVA Agentic OS, AttackIQ has introduced the industry’s first agentic operating system purpose-built for CTEM, enabling organizations to execute Continuous Threat Exposure Management autonomously at enterprise scale.

By orchestrating specialized AI agents across threat intelligence, adversary exposure validation, security validation, detection engineering, control optimization, threat debt reduction, and AI security validation, AttackIQ transforms fragmented security activities into continuous cyber resilience.

Trusted by the world’s largest enterprises, government agencies, and managed security providers, AttackIQ empowers organizations to continuously discover, validate, and reduce cyber risk with confidence.

Latest Update: Improving Human Impersonation, as the Web Closes Up Against AI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Web scraping used to be a more casual affair: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) routines created on a write-once, run-many basis – humans recording their browsing actions, refining them through various automation processes, and setting them to run at intervals, unattended, in order to obtain data from websites that only want real humans (or paying clients) accessing them and their data – and which take measures to repel automated browsing of this kind.

  • Since publicly-available data has become a truly valuable resource for AI companies (rather than the insipid ‘Data is the newly introduced gold’ rhetoric of ten years ago), at least 60% of reputable sites have been found to be repelling an AI crawler – a rise (in 2025) from 23%, two years earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Web scraping used to be a more casual affair: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) routines created on a write-once, run-many basis – humans recording their browsing actions, refining them through various automation processes, and setting them to run at intervals, unattended, in order to obtain data from websites that only want real humans (or paying clients) accessing them and their data – and which take measures to repel automated browsing of this kind.

Sources indicate that of course, domains subject to this treatment often considered RPA to be more akin to ‘data exfiltration’ and/or ‘hacking’ than any definition of ‘browsing’. Prior to the current era of AI, web scraping emerged from obscurity quite rarely, as a marginal form of pest; until LinkedIn debuted an ultimately-doomed lawsuit against HiQ Labs, an ‘intelligent automation’ provider, and one of many corporate concerns that challenged LinkedIn’s right to harvest publicly, profit privately.

Since publicly-available data has become a truly valuable resource for AI companies (rather than the insipid ‘Data is the newly introduced gold’ rhetoric of ten years ago), at least 60% of reputable sites have been found to be repelling an AI crawler – a rise (in 2025) from 23%, two years earlier.

In practical terms, defending against any kind of web scraper is about pattern-matching, and looking for evidence of algorithmic access, such as screenshotting non-selectable text, or polling the CSS stylesheets, or the other underlying structures of a page.

These actions in themselves, no matter who or what executes them, are often considered evidence of automated processes rather than human interaction; personally – and especially at Yandex – I often have to complete CAPTCHAs because I make ‘uncommon’ or technical queries; and the more protective and protected domains are generally intolerant of anything but ‘mom ‘n pop’ baseline browsing behavior.

Sources indicate that however, that’s still a relatively rare and heavy-handed experience. For the most part, anti-scraper logic and algorithms are looking not so much at the actions as for the way they are enacted – and especially for repetitive usage patterns for keyboard and mouse interaction. This could mean that a played-back RPA human interaction that works at first will shortly become blacklisted, because its lack of variation reveals it over time as a routine, and not a person.

Because of the growth of AI scraping, the tools of the RPA industry have suddenly become of great interest both to AI and intelligence companies that consider publicly available data ‘fair game’ in spite of any interstitial defenses (a stance theoretically supported by LinkedIn’s defeat in the aforementioned lawsuit – at least in the US); and the defending domains that in most (but not all) cases don’t have quite enough market capture to retain their profitable user base behind a login-wall, and would prefer to keep access open.

In the latter case, the companies have hardened themselves against the customary dedicated ‘headless’ browsers common in RPA, and against dedicated RPA frameworks such as Microsoft’s Playwright, and its derivatives and forks.

According to recent reports, the security sector has taken an interest lately in whether AI-powered web agents can actually still be recognized by sites that are on the defensive against such activities. After all, these incursions may not be running on a CRON job, but neither are they ‘human’.

In this regard, a newly introduced paper† from Canada proposes an AI-powered web agent designed to test the effectiveness of current anti-bot defenses. By combining a modified version of Chromium with AI models trained to reproduce human mouse and keyboard activity, the new system achieved access (non-rejection of browsing) in 89% of tests on a benchmark of protected websites – 12 percentage points above the best previously-published result:.

Comparative test results for bypassing eleven categories of web bot protection. Figures indicate successful page access as percentages, with test counts in parentheses. The fresh paper’s system, DarkAgent, achieved the highest overall score across 80 tests, compared with previously published results for nine other browser configurations. Source.

The system, dubbed DarkAgent, consists of Browsium, a customized Chromium browser engineered to conceal evidence of automated control; and Behavium, a framework incorporating two machine learning models: MouseGen, and KeyboardGen, which, together, simulate human interaction with the browser:.

The DarkAgent workflow. Browsing decisions are translated into simulated human interactions, executed through Browsium’s native input mechanisms. The resulting page changes are fed back to the planning agent to determine its next action.

The architecture, shown above, addresses four categories of evidence available to bot detection systems, namely interaction patterns; browser and device characteristics; evidence of automated browser control; and network protocol characteristics.

The aforementioned KeyboardGen was trained on the Aalto keyboard dataset, derived from a study of 136 million keystrokes, to reproduce typing rhythms, errors and corrections. MouseGen was trained on the Boğaziçi Mouse Dynamics dataset, with additional scrolling data sourced from the Attentive Cursor dataset:.

Examples of mouse movements, in coordinate and interpreted form, from the Attentive Cursor Dataset. Source.

Industry observers note that both generators use Transformer architectures, while the browser modifications were implemented through conventional programming. OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 was used to decide which actions to perform during the benchmark tests.

In a recent development, the browser’s reported identity and the simulated user behavior are coordinated throughout each session, so that the various signals presented to a website remain consistent with one another. To support this, a separate JavaScript-based environment within Chromium allows the agent to inspect web pages without exposing its presence to the website’s own scripts:.

Comparison of conventional browser automation (top), using the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) to inspect and control web pages, and the latest paper’s approach (bottom), where a private communication channel reduces the evidence of automated activity visible to websites.

It has been revealed that the simulated mouse movements and keystrokes are then processed by the browser as genuine user input, with the same trusted status granted to physical mouse and keyboard activity. Variations in mouse trajectories and typing patterns, learned from recorded human activity, facilitate different sequences of movements and actin timings, reflecting the natural inconsistencies of human interaction.

DarkAgent was evaluated using Stealth Bench V1, a benchmark developed by Browser Use, comprising 80 short mouse and keyboard tasks on live websites, requiring no login and covering eleven categories of protection: Cloudflare; PerimeterX; DataDome; Akamai; reCAPTCHA; Kasada; Shape; GeeTest; hCaptcha; Temu; and (unspecified) site-specific anti-bot systems.

Industry observers note that the tests were conducted in August 2026*, using geographically-matched residential proxies, with success measured solely by whether page access was obtained, and discounting task completion. Comparative results were drawn from earlier baseline tests conducted by the benchmark’s authors.

To establish the individual contributions of DarkAgent’s components, 30 browsing sessions were scheduled for each of 18 configurations on a website hosted by the researchers, with identical prompts, tasks, planning models, and limits on the number of actions.

For this, standard Chromium and Browsium were tested with and without Behavium, and with MouseGen and KeyboardGen enabled independently.

Additional comparisons were made with Firefox; Camoufox; the Playwright derivative Patchright; CloakBrowser; and publicly-available human behavior simulators Ghost Cursor; HumanTyping; and CloakBrowser’s Humanize.

The browsing sessions were evaluated using FP-Agent (an existing bot-detection system); additionally, JA4DB (a database of network connection fingerprints) was used to check whether the browser’s reported identity was consistent with its network activity.

Beyond the initial Stealth Bench V1 results presented earlier, all browsing sessions conducted without behavioral simulation were identified as automated by FP-Agent, while every session conducted with Behavium enabled in either Chromium or Browsium was classified as human:.

Bot detection results across 18 browser configurations, based on 30 sessions per configuration. P(Human) indicates the average probability of human activity assigned by FP-Agent, Verdict indicates the most frequent classification, and the final column identifies the browser engine inferred from the network connection.

Similar results were obtained with Ghost Cursor and CloakBrowser’s Humanize, indicative of a weakness in FP-Agent (which doesn’t examine how fast the mouse moves, or how its speed changes).

In a recent development, in AgentShield tests, all 139 form-filling sessions from the benchmark’s existing automated agents were flagged as bot activity, as were all ten sessions conducted with Browsium using standard automated input. With DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize, all ten trials per configuration were completed successfully without detection:.

According to recent reports, results of the AgentShield form-completion tests, showing successful submissions, bot detection rates, detection scores, mouse movements and keypress durations. DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize escaped detection, though DarkAgent’s keypress durations were considerably closer to those of human people.

When new fields appeared in the form, they were attended to by DarkAgent within an average of 3.74 seconds, compared to 4.72 seconds for human users. The greater variation in human response times suggests, the authors contend, that bots could still be identified by the length and consistency of the pauses between actions.

Although this almost-impenetrable paper is not likely to gather many adherents to the cause, web scraping is one of the most interesting challenges for the dataset-builder and proponent of agentic AI.

However, it’s fast-becoming a Quixotic pursuit; even sites that may be indifferent to data acquisition routines are now likely to become defended against RPA and agentic AI in the very near future, simply because it is becoming a default position.

While data of the kind dealt with in this research can be extracted from human engagement farms in Asia, such data will inevitably form recognizable patterns in the aggregate, so that the routines that are part of them can be specifically blocked – a familiar pattern in a latest cold war that’s starting to heat up.

Projecting the scenario to an extreme, truly effective RPA countermeasures could signal the wholesale revival of the crowdsourced worker – lately an eclipsed figure.

† Titled ‘Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion’.

* Relevant only because GPT4.1 was available then.

Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token.
  • According to recent reports, expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck.
  • Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least vital experts (in each layer independently).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

According to recent reports, expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least vital experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

According to recent reports, our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

According to recent reports, in this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

In a recent development, this means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective).

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:.

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error.

Recent findings suggest that because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:.

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:.

Industry observers note that this F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

Sources indicate that what does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:.

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

It has been revealed that in terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Sources indicate that notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

Industry observers note that we evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

In a recent development, across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more notable. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub concerns autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

Recent findings suggest that we created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

Industry observers note that this command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:.

Sources indicate that HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916.

Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

According to recent reports, A busy channel is good at surfacing a request and much less reliable as a delivery initiative. Slack and ClickUp overlap more than a simple chat-versus-tasks comparison suggests: Slack has Lists and workflows, while ClickUp includes Chat and collaborative Docs. The decision is which environment should organize the team’s daily work.

Choose Slack when your biggest need is communication across departments and the tools you already use. Choose ClickUp when tasks, dependencies, time, and reporting need one accountable home. We prefer ClickUp as the delivery system for a project-heavy team, with Slack retained when its wider communication network already has value.

Industry observers note that both products appear in our best AI collaboration tools guide. This comparison evaluates where each belongs in a real team workflow, including where using them together is more useful than replacing one with the other.

Consider a product team preparing a website launch. Design must finish before development, copy needs approval, and analytics must be ready before release. A marketing lead needs a quick answer about launch risk, while individual contributors need to know what to do next.

Slack is a natural place to create the launch channel, bring design and engineering into the same thread, and capture the decision behind a change. A Slack list can assign small follow-ups with dates and status. A canvas can keep the brief and key links visible, reducing the time upcoming participants spend asking for context.

ClickUp gives the launch a more explicit delivery structure. Tasks can carry an assignee, due date, status, and custom fields; subtasks separate work that belongs under a larger deliverable. Dependencies make the relationship between design, development, and approval more visible. A manager can move between a task list and a schedule view without reconstructing the blueprint from messages.

For a small, straightforward launch, Slack Lists may be enough. Our recommendation moves toward ClickUp when there are repeated handoffs, several launches, or a need to track effort and report progress consistently. ClickUp’s flexibility brings setup work of its own: too many statuses and custom fields make a simple project harder to use.

In Slack, a useful AI request starts with work the team has already discussed: summarize the open questions, explain a decision, or prepare a brief for someone joining the project. Slackbot’s value comes from the relevant context it can access, not from replacing an accountable owner. The official example below demonstrates research being organized into a canvas; it is a vendor product example, not a result from our own test.

Industry observers note that clickUp Brain can work with project context, and the action-item menu shown below illustrates the connection between writing and follow-up work. The useful result is a proposed set of actions that a team can assign and refine. For the launch example, we would keep those actions in the project so that a summary and the delivery record do not drift apart.

Slack is the stronger choice when the question is who remarked what, why a decision changed, or which colleague needs to join the discussion. ClickUp is the stronger starting point when the output needs to become managed project work. Neither AI output settles a dependency or commits a deadline on its own; a project owner still needs to approve the change.

Recent findings suggest that plan choice matters for this workflow. Slack Free and Pro provide a limited Slackbot preview; Business+ includes 15 messages per member each week, with additional usage available through the applicable credit arrangement. Permission and connected-app scope determine what the assistant can use. A paid communication plan and unrestricted AI usage are different purchases.

Slack’s official overview below highlights how AI fits into the communication workspace. Use it to understand the product’s approach alongside the concrete work examples above.

According to recent reports, slack AI | AI that works where you do. Video: Slack.

The ClickUp overview provides a second view of the decision: how AI can support project follow-through rather than just summarize discussion.

It has been revealed that how to Streamline Project Management With ClickUp Brain. Video: ClickUp.

ClickUp’s Slack integration can create tasks from messages, show rich previews, and post activity updates to chosen channels. That supports a practical handoff: a customer matter arrives in Slack, someone turns it into a ClickUp task, and the channel receives meaningful progress changes rather than a second manually maintained task list.

Sources indicate that use one authoritative task record. If the same deliverable lives independently in a Slack list and a ClickUp task, somebody will eventually revision only one. ClickUp documents the integration as available across plans, but particular automation and connected-search capabilities have their own plan requirements. An integration is also not permission for every user to see every private task.

It has been revealed that the examples below use standard USD annual-billing rates, expressed as a monthly equivalent. They exclude tax, temporary promotions, and additional AI usage. Annual billing means paying the annual commitment, rather than buying a month at the displayed equivalent.

For ten people, Slack Pro plus ClickUp Core comes to a $162.50 monthly equivalent, or $1,950 billed annually, before tax and optional usage. Slack Pro plus ClickUp Business is $242.50 per month equivalent, or $2,910 per year. The combined stack is easier to justify when Slack already connects departments or external collaborators beyond the project team.

Sources indicate that clickUp’s current Core pricing includes a Brain trial, while Business includes Brain with a pooled credit allowance. Do not treat a trial label as a permanent unlimited AI entitlement. Slack Pro is also different from Business+ for ongoing Slackbot use. For an AI-centered comparison, the higher tiers and actual credit consumption matter more than the cheapest paid seat.

According to recent reports, choose Slack if colleagues need a better way to coordinate, ask questions, and act on information from several business tools. Its strongest case is a team whose work already spans departments and needs a shared communication layer.

Choose ClickUp if work has dependencies, time tracking, repeated assignments, or reporting needs that outgrow a lightweight list. Its integrated Chat may also reduce the need for a separate messenger within a self-contained project team.

We recommend Slack for teams whose coordination spans many departments and business tools, and ClickUp for teams whose main problem is executing projects reliably. For an established Slack organization, connecting ClickUp is often a better move than migrating every conversation just to improve task management.

Decision Models in Hugging Face

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text.
  • Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.
  • "I was charged twice for my subscription.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.".

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

Sources indicate that A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

It has been revealed that the community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models).

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:.

Sources indicate that we could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:.

Sources indicate that A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

In a recent development, zero-shot classification addresses an crucial part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

Consider these three approaches:.

In a recent development, the advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:.

Industry observers note that the state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Sources indicate that questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:.

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

According to recent reports, the model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:.

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​.

Here, KKK is the number of choices.

Consider this illustrative distribution:.

It has been revealed that ∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:.

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​.

In a recent development, in this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

How urgent is this customer request?

The model again produces a probability distribution:.

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:.

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​.

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7.

The reported score is therefore 1.7.

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Is the customer requesting a refund?

It has been revealed that rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Let YYY represent a binary outcome:.

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p).

In a recent development, P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

It has been revealed that the model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:.

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​.

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:.

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997.

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

According to recent reports, decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:.

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

According to recent reports, transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:.

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:.

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:.

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a latest model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:.

The default server runs on port 9931.

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it reveals the parts that matter:.

In a recent development, first-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Industry observers note that traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that states whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator.

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

According to recent reports, the advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.
