LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens.
  • In a recent development, to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models.
  • Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

In a recent development, to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

Industry observers note that JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

Sources indicate that LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):.

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

In a recent development, indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

Sources indicate that in short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

It has been revealed that LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

Industry observers note that LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the upcoming vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

Industry observers note that that's really awesome! With an Apple pkl community renderer, you could potentially write PKL and render LLMON. 🥒🍋.

Any-to-pkl-community will convert json, yaml, toml to pkl, so just need the render part.

According to recent reports, this is an interesting development, especially the idea of giving LLMs a more explicit structure for understanding instructions, data, and their relationships. The discussion about prompt injection and separating instructions from input data is particularly relevant as organizations build more advanced LLM applications. Implementing these approaches requires engineers who understand model behavior, fine-tuning, context management, and evaluation. I think these technical requirements are vital when estimating the cost to hire an LLM engineer, particularly for specialized enterprise projects. I came across this resource that explores the different factors involved: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/cost-to-hire-llm-engineer-2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month. If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist. In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.What is SEMrush? SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database. The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension Features Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in significant sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords. All SEMrush customers receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons neededMost accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring. Ahrefs Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The firm was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database. Features Backlink alerts data and upcoming keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.Domain ComparisonReports with charts and graphsJavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO complications.A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis. User Interface Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need rapidly. In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks. AHREFS The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs. Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include: You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlinkJumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation. SEMRUSH When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic. You'll also find some other options like A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting. WHO WINS? Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources. When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both. Rank Tracking If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors. Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job. Ahrefs The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter. Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers: You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty. It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not. SEMRUSH SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool: All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking. Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages. Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report. WHO WINS? Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords. SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment. Keyword Research Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now. When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms. AHREFS The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine. Ahrefs supports several features, including: It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use. SEMRUSH SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear. The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to: Show performance metrics by keywordSearch results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keywordSEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords. WHO WINS? Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike. If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations. Competitor Analysis Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you. AHREFS Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also indicates you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more. Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have. To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours. SEMRUSH SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including: Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites. SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more. The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets. WHO WINS? SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition. When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose. Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Ransomware isn't slowing down. A upcoming framework gives security teams the edge to trace attackers back to their source.

Recent findings suggest that it's a now-familiar scenario: "Warning" abruptly displays on the computer screen as the system locks down. A ransom note follows, threatening data extortion and continued disruptions if a demand is not met. Although it may seem sudden at the moment, the attack was actually the final step in what may have been years of planning, all carried out by a sprawling, interconnected network of underground actors.

In a recent development, but a newly introduced framework based on an identity graph analysis, developed by Flare threat researcher Assaf Morag, aims to help defenders and law enforcement take a more proactive approach to ransomware risk by better understanding who they're up against. When applied during research, the framework can uncover the inner workings of these operations, including indicators of compromise (IoCs) that are critical to incident-response investigations. Researchers can also use it to find connections among various threat actors and groups, which is increasingly important as new groups emerge each year.

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up.

Sources indicate that mapping and understanding the connections among the various ransomware gangs is also vital when it comes to documenting the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that ransomware groups use against organizations daily. Threat actors are highly adaptable, developing, buying, or renting fresh tools all the time to bypass endpoint detection and response (EDR) and to craft more convincing phishing emails. So the more available data about their operations, the more predictable their behaviors become for defenders.

Morag plans to debut his repeatable investigative methodology for mapping criminal organizations in a briefing at Black Hat Europe 2026. He will walk through the framework step by step; anyone can use it to reproduce the research or apply the same process to a new investigation.

Sources indicate that building a framework wasn't Morag's original goal. He first set out to study how initial access brokers (IABs) operate on Dark Web forums. But he realized the interconnected web of threat actors was too vast to dissect using available resources. His efforts to connect gang operators and affiliates to IABs actually took two long months of manual work, which wasn't a useful process for such a swiftly moving threat landscape. That's when Morag decided to develop a framework to help graph the activity. Once it was ready, the same research took only three hours.

Sources indicate that to build the framework, Morag went into detective mode, gathering clues from forums and chat posts and sorting them into various buckets for "hard evidence" versus "soft evidence." The first included factors like specific messaging IDs, emails, or chat handles, while writing styles, typos, and reused phrases fell into the latter. Once he was able to verify a clue, he could use it to search for other connections. Eventually, the confirmations expanded into a massive map of connected identities with 21 personae, active over 17 years, with 5,437 posts.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure.

Sources indicate that morag's findings support how ransomware attacks are rarely conducted by a single group from start to finish, and how operations often mirror legitimate businesses with everyone playing their role. That makes it hard to parse out exactly who's who.

According to recent reports, that became obvious when Morag came across a notification posted to a Dark Web forum, translated from Russian, that read, "We are the oldest international Russian ransomware affiliate program." The group claimed to be a private program that emerged in 2018. But based on underground forum discussions, he noticed that some members had been active since 2010.

Tracking Tox IDs was the primary way Morag traced the connections, unveiling the true identity behind the fake personae and generic aliases threat actors use, like "John" or "Michael." Ransomware ecosystems commonly use communication platforms like Tox, Discord, Telegram, and Jabber to conduct payment negotiations with organizations or to recruit new affiliates, among other actions.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper.

According to recent reports, when communicating with someone through a specific Tox address, Morag knew he was reaching one consistent endpoint, whether cloud-based or someone's personal computer. Either way, it's the same device every time, which matters because threat actors often operate under multiple aliases.

"He can change his name, but if I can take these identifiers and connect them together, that could be a way to look beyond the persona's name, which is usually fake, and that's exactly what I did," Morag tells Dark Reading.

During the course of investigation, Morag discovered six layers of operational roles across the business flow:.

The homemade ransom layer: Useful for defenders to study, these are the people who develop ransomware strains, loader malware that bypasses antivirus and EDR, and infostealer payloads.

The ransom deployment layer: The gang operators and their affiliates who select the ransomware/malware, deploy it, and extort the victims.

Pen-testers: Folks who probe for weaknesses to find ways into organizations.

The dealers: IABs that buy and sell that initial access, like a sales department for cybercrime. (Morag was able to pinpoint seven individuals active for over nine years, spanning 50 forums and a whopping 1,300 events.).

Fraud recovery: Organizations that perform diagnostics, negotiate with attackers, and arrange settlements with victims.

Crypto draining: Those that process stolen seed phrases and private keys at scale and cross-sell crypto services to ransomware victims to compromise and drain wallets.

Industry observers note that while piecing it together, one link particularly surprised Morag: a tie between supposed good-guy fraud-recovery firms and the ransomware deployers. Companies claim to help ransomware victims but secretly defraud them, he notes, and victim organizations have no clue.

Up until the fraud recovery layer in the business flow, everything was done in Russian. After that, Morag noticed an intentional switch to the English language. Once the ransomware locked an organization's system down, the ransomware deployers swooped in, posing as legitimate businesses looking to provide recovery services. They installed tools on victims' systems, ran diagnostics, offered data recovery, and legal compliance services, Morag claims.

"This is not upcoming, and we've also seen a few cases in the past month in the US. These kinds of organizations that help other organizations fight against ransomware were actually defrauding them," Morag explains. "I haven't seen anyone make the connection between those who do the recovery fraud and those that actually deploy the ransom, which is really amazing.".

It has been revealed that while deep in the underground forums, it also became clear to Morag how much threat actors value their reputations. For instance, on Exploit, "a reputable Russian market" where attackers pay $100 to $150 and undergo a test to get in, Morag observed infighting as threat actors accused one another of not being legitimate. The forum is a place where "you don’t want to lose your reputation" or your access, he stresses, because it's where threat actors discuss sensitive dealings, such as zero-day and known vulnerability exploits, and forge latest ransomware-as-a-service partnerships. Looking into these disputes offered critical intelligence about how operations run because threat actors will throw each other under the bus by revealing what tools they use, how they move money, or what access they are trading.

Exploit, Morag says, is "a real gold mine because it explains how they work, what they're doing, the level of leadership, and who reports to who.".

Exploit was one of more than 40 underground forums he visited that, when analyzed together with the framework, revealed the inner workings of cybercrime gangs. Unmasking the players provides more evidence for organizations to fight back against ransomware as the threat disrupts everything, from Coca-Cola production to Japanese frozen food.

Industry observers note that the framework can't directly help organizations push back against ransomware, but it does provide much-needed contextual data for the private and public sectors as problems persist. Morag is applying the framework to help with attacks against financial systems — an obviously huge target for threat actors — for example. He also applied it to investigate another ransomware group more recently and says it yielded helpful results.

Real insight into a large operation like the one Morag discovered, knowing it included a fake fraud recovery layer, may also make organizations think twice about negotiating. They never know who's on the other line.

"It's [about] knowing your enemy," Morag says.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Recent findings suggest that today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

In a recent development, the router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise aims include monthly credits for compute and inference.

Industry observers note that on OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

Recent findings suggest that the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

Industry observers note that openRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

According to recent reports, when a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Industry observers note that before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

Sources indicate that routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Industry observers note that pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO customers get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

Sources indicate that on model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two fresh tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics highlights the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

According to recent reports, requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

Sources indicate that this is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license.
  • audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.
  • In a recent development, rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

In a recent development, rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

According to recent reports, on-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

In a recent development, on the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software.
  • Recent findings suggest that just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild.
  • According to recent reports, windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Recent findings suggest that just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

According to recent reports, windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable mentioned the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly stated.

In a recent development, which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
  • I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
  • Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

It has been revealed that I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

Industry observers note that that's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Industry observers note that before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

In a recent development, llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

Sources indicate that offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

In a recent development, if the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

Industry observers note that first version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

In a recent development, the fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Industry observers note that experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

Industry observers note that the API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization proposal of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

Industry observers note that the conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

Sources indicate that the model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

Industry observers note that I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

According to recent reports, most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

Sources indicate that it runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Recent findings suggest that transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

In a recent development, beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

Recent findings suggest that the generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
  • Recent findings suggest that heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Recent findings suggest that heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

In a recent development, the blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis mentioned the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

Sources indicate that “Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”.

In a recent development, the Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted latest “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Sources indicate that richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are crucial because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”.

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders noted.

Recent findings suggest that sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, Upcoming Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Recent findings suggest that where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent firm Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

#138135. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1385 w)

Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1385 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
  • A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
  • Sources indicate that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

Sources indicate that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

It has been revealed that better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

According to recent reports, we wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

Recent findings suggest that the short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

Recent findings suggest that this is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

Industry observers note that these overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

In a recent development, we treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

In a recent development, distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That states nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

Industry observers note that one caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

According to recent reports, out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

In a recent development, more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can proposal around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

Dharma-AI R&D · We Make AI Your Model.

💡 Key Takeaways
